What Is a JWT?

A signed, self-contained ticket a client carries with every request — instead of a session Laravel keeps on the server.

Laravel's default session-based login keeps almost everything on the server: log in, and Laravel stores "this session belongs to user 7" in its own session store, handing the browser only a small opaque cookie that means nothing on its own — every later request looks that cookie up against the server's session store to find out who's making it. That's a natural fit for a framework serving full HTML pages back to a browser that already holds a cookie jar.

A JSON API being called from anywhere — a script, a mobile app, eventually this project's own React frontend — doesn't have quite the same natural fit, and this project reaches for a different shape entirely: a JWT (JSON Web Token). Log in, and the client gets back a token that already contains "this is user 7, role customer" — signed by the server, but not stored by the server at all. Every later request carries that same token (next topic covers exactly how), and the server just re-checks the signature to trust what's inside it, rather than looking anything up. Nothing about "who is this" lives in server memory or a database row between requests — that's what stateless means here, and it's the whole reason a JWT needs no server-side session store to work at all.

A JWT's own shape is three dot-separated, base64-encoded parts — header.payload.signature — but only one of those matters for how this project uses it: the payload, a plain JSON object (here, just { sub: userId, role } — the next topic shows exactly where that comes from) that's easy to decode and read, by anyone, without needing the signing secret at all. That's worth sitting with: a JWT is signed, not encrypted — tamper-proof, in that changing the payload invalidates the signature, but never secret. Nothing sensitive (a password, anything you wouldn't want a curious user peeking at their own token to see) belongs in one.
